title: Delta-sigma noise shaping for low-resolution quantization in Gaussian-modulated continuous-variable quantum key distribution
authors: Wenjun Fan, Zhenlin Zhao, Dawei Wang
abstract: Low-resolution digital-to-analog conversion can simplify continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CVQKD) transmitters, but coarse quantization increases excess noise and can generate data-correlated spectral replicas. We demonstrate digital delta--sigma modulation (DSM) for low-resolution waveform generation in Gaussian-modulated CVQKD. In a 500-MBaud CVQKD system over 20~km of fiber, 3-bit second-order DSM achieves an estimated asymptotic secret key rate of 46.38~Mbps at an oversampling ratio of 12, whereas uniform quantization yields no positive rate. With 4-bit second-order DSM, the rate reaches 50.11~Mbps, approximately 97\% of the 12-bit reference. A noise model combining the DSM noise-transfer function with matched filtering guides the sampling-rate and signal-band design for effective noise suppression. We also identify a phase-conjugate spectral replica arising from third-order intermodulation between the pilot tone and quantum signal, and evaluate its key-rate penalty using a linear-replica security model. At 3-bit resolution and an oversampling ratio of 24, first-order DSM reduces the experimentally estimated leakage-mode strength by approximately four orders of magnitude. Together, our findings establish the security boundaries and operating conditions of DSM, providing design guidance for low-resolution CVQKD transmitters.
summary: This paper introduces and validates the use of digital delta-sigma modulation (DSM) to mitigate noise and spectral artifacts arising from low-resolution quantization in CVQKD transmitters. By effectively shaping the quantization noise, DSM allows the system to maintain high secret key rates even when using cost-saving, low-bit-depth components. This provides essential design guidance for practical, long-distance quantum communication links.
main_problem: The paper addresses the performance degradation and excess noise introduced by using low-resolution digital-to-analog converters (DACs) in Continuous-Variable Quantum Key Distribution (CVQKD) transmitters.
main_result: Implementing digital delta-sigma modulation (DSM) significantly suppresses quantization noise, allowing low-resolution systems to achieve high secret key rates, approaching those of full-resolution systems.
method: The authors model the quantization error using DSM structures (first- and second-order) and analyze the resulting noise transfer function (NTF) to quantify noise suppression and spectral replica penalties.
model_or_system: The system is a Gaussian-modulated CVQKD link transmitting over optical fiber. The core model involves analyzing the quantization noise introduced by low-resolution DACs and its impact on the secret key rate.
key_observables: Asymptotic secret key rate (Mbps), Signal-to-Quantization-Noise Ratio (SQNR), and leakage-mode strength reduction.
important_parameters: Quantizer resolution (e.g., 3-bit, 4-bit), Oversampling Ratio (OSR), and DSM order (first-order, second-order).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a linearized additive quantization-error model and assumes specific noise distributions for the quantization error.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structure of DSMs and the theoretical noise transfer function (NTF) magnitude, showing noise suppression in the signal band. Other figures compare SQNR vs. OSR and show the reduction of leakage-mode strength.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the problem of low-resolution quantization in CVQKD. It then develops the theoretical framework using DSMs to model noise shaping, derives the key performance metrics (SQNR, key rate), and finally presents quantitative results comparing DSM performance against uniform quantization across varying resolutions and OSRs.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles practical hardware limitations (low-resolution DACs) in quantum communication protocols, providing crucial design guidelines for building real-world quantum networks.
